Read About Ho Chi Minh City

A city that has been renamed by nearly every power that ever held it, and still answers to both of its names at once.

A city with two names

Ask a taxi driver to take you to "Ho Chi Minh City" and he'll understand you fine, but almost nobody who lives here actually calls it that. It's Saigon — in conversation, on shopfronts, on the sports jerseys, in the name of the beer. The renaming happened in 1976, after reunification, to honor the revolutionary leader who never lived to see North and South Vietnam become one country. But the old name never left, and in 2025 the government made that split official rather than fighting it: Vietnam's administrative reforms restored "Saigon" as the formal name of the city's own central ward, so the metropolis is Ho Chi Minh City and its historic heart is Saigon again, both on paper now, not just in speech.

Before it was Saigon, it was Prey Nokor, a Khmer fishing settlement built on ground the Cambodians had taken from a Cham village called Baigaur. Vietnamese settlers arriving in the 1600s Vietnamized the Khmer name into "Sài Gòn," and for a while, under the Nguyen lords, the place was officially called Gia Dinh instead — Sài Gòn only came back into administrative use once the French took the city by force in 1859 and needed a name their own maps could carry. So the sequence runs: a Cham village, a Khmer fishing town, a Vietnamese frontier post, a French colonial capital, the capital of an independent South Vietnam, and finally a reunified nation's second city named for the man who reunified it. Almost no city changes hands, and names, that many times and keeps functioning the whole way through.

Cholon, the city inside the city

Ride southwest into District 5 and the shopfront signs start carrying Chinese characters alongside the Vietnamese, the incense coils get bigger, and you're in Cholon — a name that simply means "big market," after a market here once so much larger than its older neighbor that people started calling it that instead of anything else. Cholon was founded and built almost entirely by the Hoa, ethnic Chinese who settled the delta from the 1600s onward, many of them Ming-dynasty loyalists who fled south rather than live under the Qing. By the 1800s it had grown into its own separate walled city, complete with its own governor, and for decades Saigon and Cholon developed side by side as twin cities joined by a canal, not one metropolis.

They weren't merged into a single administrative area until 1931, under the cumbersome French title "Saigon–Cholon," and even then the fused name never caught on in everyday speech — people kept calling the two halves by their old names, the way New Yorkers still say "Brooklyn" and mean something distinct from "Manhattan" even though both have been one city for over a century. Cholon's Chinese community calls their neighborhood Dī'àn instead, "the embankment," a name that goes back to a literal flood levee built to hold back the same canal that once separated the two cities. Walk Thien Hau Temple's incense-thick hall today and you're standing in what was, for most of its history, a foreign city's Chinatown grafted onto Vietnam's largest port — not a themed district built for visitors, but the actual, functioning old town of a community that got here under its own power and never left.

Cholon and Saigon developed side by side as twin cities joined by a canal for most of the 19th century — not one metropolis, but two.

A city built to float

Long before anyone paved a road here, the entire settlement moved by water. The Saigon River and the canal network branching off it — the khlong, in the regional term the French inherited — carried the city's boats, markets, and houses long before it carried its cars. Early Saigon was a floating town: merchants living on rafts, produce sold boat-to-boat, whole neighborhoods organized around canal frontage rather than street frontage. The French, once they took the city, drained and filled a great deal of that canal network to build the boulevard grid that still defines District 1 today — but they didn't erase the logic entirely. The Saigon River still does real freight work for one of Southeast Asia's busiest container ports, and the newer Saigon Waterbus line, spun up to relieve District 1's traffic, is in its own small way a return to the city's oldest transportation habit rather than an invention of a new one.

From ruins to reform

The years right after reunification in 1975 were harder on the city than the war that preceded them. Central planning replaced the market economy the South had run for two decades, private business was nationalized wholesale, and the resulting shortages sent hundreds of thousands of people fleeing the country by boat rather than stay and live inside the new system. It took a decade for Hanoi to admit the approach wasn't working. In 1986, the Communist Party's Sixth Congress adopted Doi Moi — literally "renovation" — a sweeping reversal that reopened the country to private enterprise and foreign investment while keeping the same one-party government in place. Ho Chi Minh City, still the country's commercial engine even after the political capital had permanently shifted to Hanoi, is where that reversal shows up first and hardest: the skyline of Bitexco and Landmark 81, the flood of small private businesses that now line every downtown street, and a GDP that today accounts for roughly a quarter of the entire country's output all trace back to a decision made in a single Party congress four decades ago.

The sound the city makes

Ho Chi Minh City has more motorbikes registered than most countries have citizens, and the sound and rhythm of that fleet is as much a part of the place as any building on this itinerary. At rush hour the traffic doesn't stop so much as it flows continuously around itself, a river of scooters that pedestrians learn to cross not by waiting for a gap — there isn't one — but by walking at a steady, predictable pace and letting the traffic part around them, the same way you'd wade into a current rather than try to outrun it. It looks like chaos from a hotel window and feels like a negotiated agreement once you're standing in the middle of it. Almost every visitor's first real culture shock in Saigon happens on a street corner, not in a museum, and almost every visitor who stays more than a day or two ends up finding the negotiated agreement kind of beautiful.
